title: Foam on the river
hookLine: form like foam, feeling like bubbles, perception a mirage, formations a hollow stalk, consciousness a magic show (SN 22.95)

lines: ON THE BANK OF THE GANGES.
A LUMP OF FOAM, FLOATING BY.
cards: The Buddha is staying at Ayojjha, on the bank of the Ganges. The river is carrying a big lump of foam downstream. He tells the monks: suppose someone with good eyes looked closely at that foam, examined it carefully.
What would they find? Empty, hollow, nothing solid inside. Then, one after another, he names four more things a person might see in an ordinary year.

teach.b: SN 22.95 matches each of the five heaps, the parts of a person from Vajira's chariot, to something you can see. Form, the body, is like that lump of foam.
Feeling is like a bubble: in autumn, when it rains in big drops, a bubble rises on the water and bursts. Pleasant, painful, neither: up and gone.

teach.h: PERCEPTION: A MIRAGE, FORMATIONS: A PLANTAIN
teach.b: Perception, the mind's labeling, is like a mirage in the last month of the hot season, shimmering on the road, convincing, not there. Formations, our habits and intentions, are like a banana tree.
A man goes looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. He cuts down a big, straight, young plantain trunk and peels it, layer after layer, and finds no heartwood at all. Not even softwood.
And consciousness is like a magic show, a trick put on by a conjurer at a crossroads. Someone with good eyes sees through it. Each picture is chosen carefully.
Foam has a shape, but you can't build with it. Bubbles last a moment. A mirage really does look like water.
The plantain is layers all the way down. And the magic show doesn't say consciousness isn't happening; it says it isn't what it appears to be. The point isn't gloom.
One who sees this way, the Buddha says, grows disenchanted, and through dispassion is freed.
The closing verse adds a plain reminder: this body, when life, heat and consciousness leave it, lies cast aside, food for others.
Foam is still beautiful on a river. You just don't try to hold it.

how: Some Buddhists contemplate the five aggregates through images like these, and teachers in several traditions use the foam, the bubble and the mirage to teach impermanence.

o: a river current that carries all away
a mirage seen on a hot road
foam, the picture for the body

p: a mirage in the hot season

s: in SN 22.95, formations are like a banana tree with no heartwood
a man peels a plantain trunk layer by layer and finds no heartwood.
the simile says consciousness doesn't happen at all
it says consciousness is like a magic show: real as a show, not what it seems.
the Buddha gives this teaching beside the Ganges
at Ayojjha, watching foam carried by the river.

games.q: you're looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. you cut down a big plantain trunk and peel it. what do you find?
o: layers, and no heartwood at all.
games.why: just layers, not even softwood: the Buddha's picture of formations, habits and intentions with no solid core.

practice: If you can, look at foam or bubbles right now, the top of a fizzy drink, soap in the sink, a puddle in the rain; if not, picture one clearly, and watch a bubble form, sit, and burst.
Then turn to your own feelings as they come, small pleasant ones, small unpleasant ones, and see each rise and burst like raindrops on the river. No need to push any away.

wordCard.voice: Phena. The Pali word for foam, the image for the body in SN 22.95, where feeling is a bubble, perception a mirage, formations a plantain trunk, consciousness a magic show. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali phena: foam. SN 22.95 is the Phenapindupama Sutta, the simile of the lump of foam.

carryVoice: Your line: up and gone. Five pictures, and nothing solid to grab in any of them. Day six hundred forty-six.
